outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the bounds on r_k(N) have moved in several places but its growth rate has not been determined: Behrend-type lower-bound constants for k=3 improved (Hunter, 29 Jan 2024; Elsholtz–Hunter–Proske–Sauermann, 18 Jun 2024); the upper bound for every k≥5 became N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}) (Leng–Sah–Sawhney, 28 Feb 2024); the k=3 upper-bound exponent rose to 1/6 (Raghavan, 27 Mar 2026); and OpenAI's repository of 6 Oct 2026 contains a 198-page claim of quasipolynomial upper bounds r_k(N) ≤ N·exp(−(log N)^{c_k}) for every k≥3 that no named expert has yet checked and whose Lean formalisation does not state that bound.
problem_asks: The statement asks, for each fixed k (k is a parameter; k≥3 is the non-trivial range, since r_2(N)=1), to determine the growth rate of r_k(N), the largest size of a subset of {1,…,N} containing no k-term arithmetic progression, as N→∞. Unpacked: (a) an upper bound on r_k(N) for each k≥3 (of the form N·f_k(N) with f_k(N)→0); (b) a lower bound on r_k(N) for each k≥3 (of the form N·g_k(N)); (c) that these match, so the growth rate is determined. The statement does not say whether one answer is wanted for all k at once or one for each k, and does not fix a precision for the growth rate. Szemerédi's theorem, named in the bullet, supplies only r_k(N)=o(N), which is context and is not itself the growth-rate question. Wikipedia's Szemerédi's theorem article (opened, last edited 29 Apr 2026) states: 'It is an open problem to determine the exact growth rate of r_k(N).'

events.what_happened: Ben Green and Terence Tao, 'New bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, III: a polylogarithmic bound for r_4(N)' (arXiv:1705.01703), May 2017 (the Tao blog post on it is dated 5 May 2017). Gives r_4(N) ≪ N/(log N)^c for some c>0.
events.delivers: Only k=4: a polylogarithmic saving, r_4(N) ≪ N/(log N)^c. Upper bound only.
events.remains: For k=4, the exact growth rate and any matching lower bound. Nothing here for k=3 or k≥5.
events.time_since_posted: Pre-window; cited as the current best k=4 bound by Wikipedia and by erdosproblems.com/3 as read.
events.direction: Upper bound for k=4 in the direction of a smaller r_4(N). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Zander Kelley and Raghu Meka, 'Strong Bounds for 3-Progressions' (arXiv:2302.05537), v1 10 Feb 2023. Abstract: for some constant β>0, any subset of {1,…,N} of size at least 2^{−O((log N)^β)}·N contains a non-trivial 3-term progression; the previous threshold was N/(log N)^{1+c}.
events.revisions: v2 18 Jun 2023; v3 9 Aug 2023; v4 26 Sep 2023; v5 5 Jan 2024; v6 28 Oct 2024 (all revisions of a pre-window paper).
events.delivers: Only k=3: r_3(N) ≤ N·2^{−O((log N)^β)} for some β>0 (the exponent 1/12 comes from later expositions, not from the abstract read here).
events.remains: k≥4 entirely; the exact growth rate for k=3 (the gap to Behrend-type lower bounds).
events.time_since_posted: Pre-window; refined by Bloom and Sisask (Sep 2023) and by Raghavan (Mar 2026); the Bloom–Sisask exposition (arXiv:2302.07211) gives a self-contained account.
events.direction: Upper bound for k=3 with a quasipolynomial-in-log shape, in the direction of a smaller r_3(N). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Thomas Bloom and Olof Sisask, 'An improvement to the Kelley–Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions' (arXiv:2309.02353), v1 5 Sep 2023. A modification of the Kelley–Meka method: a subset of {1,…,N} with no non-trivial 3-term progression has size at most exp(−c(log N)^{1/9})·N.
events.delivers: Only k=3: r_3(N) ≤ N·exp(−c(log N)^{1/9}) for some c>0.
events.remains: k≥4; the exact growth rate for k=3.
events.time_since_posted: Pre-window; the exponent 1/9 is the value Raghavan (Mar 2026) improves.
events.direction: Upper bound for k=3 in the direction of a smaller r_3(N). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: James Leng, Ashwin Sah, Mehtaab Sawhney, 'Improved bounds for five-term arithmetic progressions' (arXiv:2312.10776), v1 17 Dec 2023. Proves r_5(N) ≪ N/exp((log log N)^c) for some c∈(0,1), using the authors' improved U^4-inverse theorem and the Heath-Brown–Szemerédi density increment as codified by Green and Tao.
events.delivers: Only k=5: r_5(N) ≪ N/exp((log log N)^c). Subsumed by the k≥5 result of arXiv:2402.17995 (next-but-one event).
events.remains: k=3, k=4, and the exact growth rate for every k.
events.time_since_posted: Pre-window; superseded for k≥5 by arXiv:2402.17995.
events.direction: Upper bound for k=5 in the direction of a smaller r_5(N). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Christian Elsholtz, Laura Proske, Lisa Sauermann, 'New lower bounds for three-term progression free sets in F_p^n' (arXiv:2401.12802), v1 23 Jan 2024. Constructs subsets of Z_m^n (m≥2 fixed, n large) and F_p^n with no 3-term progression of distinct points and size at least (cm)^n for c=0.54, beating the classical c=1/2 of Salem–Spencer (1942). No bound on subsets of {1,…,N}.
events.revisions: Only v1 listed. The arXiv abstract page of arXiv:2406.12290 says that paper replaces arXiv:2401.12802 and arXiv:2401.16106.
events.delivers: Finite-group analogue only (Z_m^n and F_p^n, k=3). Per the scope rule this is a different question from r_3(N) on {1,…,N} and is recorded as discounted. It falls before the freeze date in any case.
events.remains: All of r_3(N) over the integers, and everything for k≥4.
events.time_since_posted: About 33 months to 11 Oct 2026; no separate written verification found. Superseded by arXiv:2406.12290.
events.direction: Lower bound for progression-free sets in finite groups; cuts toward larger progression-free sets in that setting. Not about the integers.
events.object: Explicit construction in Z_m^n: a subset S of Z_m^2 of size at least (7/24)m^2 with a 'reducibility' property, lifted to a progression-free set of size (cm)^n in higher dimension (c=0.54 claimed). Explicit: the abstract describes a construction, not an existence argument.

events.what_happened: Zach Hunter, 'New lower bounds for r_3(N)' (arXiv:2401.16106), v1 submitted Monday 29 Jan 2024. Develops ideas of Elsholtz, Proske and Sauermann to construct denser subsets of {1,…,N} with no 3-term progression. Abstract: 'This gives the first quasipolynomial improvement since the original construction of Behrend.' v3 (2 Jul 2024) states that the results have been merged with Elsholtz, Proske and Sauermann (arXiv:2401.12802).
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2024; v2 30 Jan 2024; v3 2 Jul 2024 (adds the merger note; the merged paper is arXiv:2406.12290).
events.delivers: Only k=3, on the integers: a lower bound r_3(N) ≫ N·2^{−(c+o(1))·2√(2 log₂ N)} with c = √(log₂√(32/9)) ≈ 0.9567 (as stated in the v3 Theorem 1). Behrend's construction has c=1 in the same form, so this improves the constant in the Behrend-type lower bound. It is not a change to the order of exp(−c√log N). The v1 abstract, read directly, claims the improvement on {1,…,N}.
events.remains: The exact growth rate of r_3(N), i.e. the gap between this lower bound and the k=3 upper bounds. All k≥4 lower bounds, which are unchanged (Rankin 1961 and O'Bryant as cited by Wikipedia).
events.time_since_posted: About 32 months to 11 Oct 2026. The merged successor (June 2024) is the paper cited in later work; no journal reference found for either.
events.direction: Lower bound for 3-AP-free subsets of {1,…,N}, improving the Behrend constant. Cuts toward larger r_3(N). No counterexample to anything the bullet asserts.
events.object: An explicit construction of subsets of {1,…,N} free of 3-term progressions, of size N·2^{−(c+o(1))·2√(2 log₂N)} with c ≈ 0.9567 (Theorem 1 of v3). It is built by adapting the Elsholtz–Proske–Sauermann construction in place of Behrend's sphere-based set. The abstract's word 'construct' is the basis for calling it explicit; I did not check the proof line by line.

events.what_happened: James Leng, Ashwin Sah, Mehtaab Sawhney, 'Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem' (arXiv:2402.17995), v1 Wednesday 28 Feb 2024, v2 29 Feb 2024. Theorem 1.1 (html, v2): 'Fix k≥5. There is c_k∈(0,1) such that r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}).' Proof: the quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the Gowers U^k-norm (companion arXiv:2402.17994) plus the density increment strategy of Heath-Brown and Szemerédi as codified by Green and Tao. Subject areas: math.CO, math.NT.
events.revisions: v1 28 Feb 2024; v2 29 Feb 2024 (listed as the current version on the arXiv page read).
events.delivers: Restricted to k≥5. For each k≥5 it moves the upper bound on r_k(N) from Gowers' N(log log N)^{−c_k} form to N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}) with c_k∈(0,1). It does not cover k=3 or k=4. Lower bounds are not changed.
events.remains: k=3 and k=4 are not covered by this paper (k=3 is covered by the Kelley–Meka line of results; k=4 by Green–Tao). The exact growth rate for every k: the upper bound here is not matched by any lower bound, and the lower bounds for k≥4 (Rankin 1961, as cited) are unchanged.
events.time_since_posted: About 31 months to 11 Oct 2026. Wikipedia describes it as a preprint result; a Rutgers seminar announcement (April 2025) is a talk, not a verification. I found no journal reference in searches.
events.direction: Upper bound for every k≥5, in the direction of a smaller r_k(N). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: James Leng, Ashwin Sah, Mehtaab Sawhney, 'Quasipolynomial bounds on the inverse theorem for the Gowers U^{s+1}[N]-norm' (arXiv:2402.17994), v1 28 Feb 2024, v2 10 Apr 2024, v3 10 Aug 2024. Proves quasipolynomial bounds for the inverse theorem for the Gowers U^{s+1}[N] norm, following Green–Tao–Ziegler and relying on Leng's equidistribution of nilsequences. The abstract says a companion paper will use it to improve bounds on Szemerédi's theorem.
events.delivers: Not a bound on r_k(N). It is a Gowers-norm inverse theorem that is an input to arXiv:2402.17995 and is cited as an input to the 2026 OpenAI claim. Recorded as an event that does not move the quantity.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.time_since_posted: About 31 months to 11 Oct 2026; no separate verification found.
events.direction: Does not bear on the direction of r_k(N); a tool result.

events.what_happened: Christian Elsholtz, Zach Hunter, Laura Proske, Lisa Sauermann, 'Improving Behrend's construction: Sets without arithmetic progressions in integers and over finite fields' (arXiv:2406.12290), v1 18 Jun 2024. Theorem 1.1 (integers): r_3(N) ≥ N·2^{−(C+o(1))√(log₂N)} with C = 2√(log₂(24/7)) < 2√2 (my arithmetic: C ≈ 2.667, against Behrend's 2√2 ≈ 2.828). Theorems 1.1–1.2 for F_p^n and Z_m^n. The abstract page comment says the paper replaces arXiv:2401.12802 and arXiv:2401.16106.
events.revisions: Only v1 listed on the arXiv abstract page read.
events.delivers: Only k=3, on the integers: a lower bound r_3(N) ≥ N·2^{−(C+o(1))√(log₂N)} with C ≈ 2.667, an improvement of the Behrend constant (the paper calls it the first improvement beyond lower-order factors, and a quasipolynomial improvement). The F_p^n and Z_m^n parts are finite analogues and are discounted for this bullet.
events.remains: The exact growth rate of r_3(N); all k≥4 lower bounds.

checked_by.who: Gil Kalai (research mathematician, combinatorics; blog 'Combinatorics and more'; affiliation not checked in this run)
checked_by.qualification: Professional combinatorialist who writes regularly on research results in the area.
checked_by.what_they_did: Blog digest (22 Jul 2024, 'Pushing Behrend Around II') of the joint paper. In the visible excerpt it describes the result for integers and the interplay with the finite-field construction; it does not describe a check of the proof, and the excerpt is truncated.

events.time_since_posted: About 28 months to 11 Oct 2026. The digest is the only qualified public engagement I found; I found no journal reference.
events.direction: Lower bound for 3-AP-free subsets of {1,…,N}, improving the Behrend constant. Cuts toward larger r_3(N). No counterexample.
events.object: Explicit construction of 3-AP-free subsets of {1,…,N} of size N·2^{−(C+o(1))√(log₂N)} with C = 2√(log₂(24/7)) ≈ 2.667, built over Z_m^n-type constructions. The paper says its integer constructions use the finite-field constructions. I did not check the proof.

events.what_happened: Michael Jaber, Yang P. Liu, Shachar Lovett, Anthony Ostuni, Mehtaab Sawhney, 'Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem' (arXiv:2504.07006), v1 9 Apr 2025. Corner-free subsets A of G×G for finite abelian G satisfy |A| ≤ |G|²·exp(−(log|G|)^{Ω(1)}).
events.delivers: A result on a different problem (the corners theorem in G×G, with applications to communication complexity). It is not about progression-free sets on {1,…,N} or r_k(N). Recorded as discounted; the method family (quasipolynomial density bounds) is related.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.time_since_posted: About 18 months to 11 Oct 2026; no verification found in searches.
events.direction: Not about the direction of r_k(N); a neighbouring theorem.

events.what_happened: Joni Teräväinen and Mengdi Wang, 'On the Green–Tao theorem for sparse sets', v1 10 Mar 2026. Quantitative Green–Tao theorem for subsets of the primes: a k-AP-free (k≥4) set of relative density δ within the primes up to N satisfies δ ≪ exp(−(log log log N)^{c_k}), improving Rimanić and Wolf.
events.delivers: Subsets of the primes, not of {1,…,N}, and relative density within the primes. A different question from r_k(N); recorded as discounted.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.time_since_posted: About 7 months to 11 Oct 2026; no verification found.
events.direction: Not about the direction of r_k(N); a neighbouring theorem on primes.

events.what_happened: Rushil Raghavan (UCLA per a search snippet; single author), 'Improved Bounds for 3-Progressions' (arXiv:2603.27045, math.NT with math.CO cross-list), v1 Friday 27 Mar 2026. Abstract: if A⊆{1,…,N} has no non-trivial 3-term progression then |A| ≤ N·exp(−c(log N)^{1/6}/log log N) for an absolute c>0. Method: an iterated version of the Kelley–Meka sifting argument, with an improved bootstrapping of Croot–Sisask almost-periodicity due to Bloom and Sisask. The paper's introduction says that upper bounds for this problem must now focus on the exponent 1/12.
events.revisions: v1 27 Mar 2026; v2 1 May 2026; v3 15 May 2026 (typo fixes, per the arXiv comments).
events.delivers: Only k=3: an upper bound on r_3(N) with exponent 1/6 on (log N), against 1/12 (Kelley–Meka) and 1/9 (Bloom–Sisask). Scope point for the judging pass: the abstract says A⊆{1,…,N}, but the html Theorem 1.4 is stated for A⊆ℤ/Nℤ with bound exp(−log(N)^{1/6−o(1)})N. Which setting carries the headline is not settled by my reading.
events.remains: Exact growth rate for k=3 (the Behrend-type lower bound is unchanged in order). All k≥4.
events.time_since_posted: About 6.5 months to 11 Oct 2026. No journal, expert note, or public check found in searches.
events.doubts: Single author with no venue yet. The setting differs between the abstract ({1,…,N}) and the html Theorem 1.4 (ℤ/Nℤ). The argument builds on the Kelley–Meka sifting method and the Bloom–Sisask bootstrapping; I did not find any public check of this preprint, and no specific error has been identified in it.
events.direction: Upper bound for k=3, in the direction of a smaller r_3(N). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Or Shalom, 'On the Furstenberg–Katznelson constant for the IP Szemerédi theorem over finite fields' (arXiv:2604.05768, math.DS with math.CO cross-list), v1 7 Apr 2026. Ergodic-theoretic constants for vector spaces over finite fields; qualitative in general, quantitative for Roth's theorem and IP-Roth over finite fields.
events.delivers: A finite-field analogue. It gives no quantitative bound for k-APs on the integers. Recorded as discounted.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.time_since_posted: About 6 months to 11 Oct 2026; no verification found.
events.direction: Not about the direction of r_k(N); a finite-field analogue.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's public repository github.com/openai/math, one commit ('Initial commit', adc7f12) dated 6 Oct 2026, includes a family (159) titled 'Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture and quasipolynomial Szemerédi bounds' with a paper 'Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions' in preprints/Quasipolynomial-Bounds-for-Arithmetic-Progressions-September-23-2026/paper.pdf. Per Thomas Bloom's erdosproblems.com blog post of 8 Oct 2026, the claim is: for k≥3 there is c_k>0 such that for large N a subset A of {1,…,N} with no non-trivial k-term progression satisfies |A| ≤ exp(−(log N)^{c_k})·N. The PDF is 198 pages, and per Bloom it appears to use the existing techniques (density increment, almost-periodicity, Kelley–Meka ideas, Gowers inverse theory, and Leng–Sah–Sawhney's inverse results). The paper also claims the reciprocal-sum consequence (Erdős Problem #3), which is outside this bullet. The PDF itself could not be read: the fetch tool returned a compressed binary.
events.revisions: None found. The folder label 'September-23-2026' is not a commit date; the folder's only commit is 6 Oct 2026. The release was described in OpenAI's research post of 6 Oct 2026, which I could not open (HTTP 403).
events.delivers: As claimed (per Bloom's blog and the erdosproblems.ai entry): an upper bound r_k(N) ≤ C_k·N·exp(−c_k·(log N)^{ε_k}) for every fixed k≥3, which is quasipolynomial in log N and for k≥4 is far stronger than Leng–Sah–Sawhney's exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}). For k=3 the shape matches Kelley–Meka; the exponent claimed is not stated in the sources I read. Restrictions carried: the claim is for k≥3 and for {1,…,N}; the reciprocal-sum consequence is claimed separately. What the Lean layer proves, on the files I read: Results/Conclusions.lean has tactic proofs (no sorry in that file) of QuantitativeDensityTheorem ∧ ReciprocalProgressionTheorem, where QuantitativeDensityBound k says r_k(N) ≤ C·N·exp(−c·(log log N)^{1+η}) for some constants (a weaker shape than the headline); the proofs depend on lemmas in about 98 imported modules under lean/OAI/Combinatorics/Progressions, which I did not inspect.
events.remains: Matching lower bounds for any k≥3 (none claimed; the lower bounds stay Behrend/Rankin-type, exp(−c√log N) for k=3 and exp(−c(log N)^{p_k}) for k≥4). The exact growth rate for every k. Also, whether the headline quasipolynomial bound is established: the sources describe it as claimed and not verified, and the formal layer as stated does not reach it.
events.time_since_posted: 5 days to 11 Oct 2026. Public engagement so far is summary and statement-level: Bloom (8 Oct) says he has 'not yet looked at in any serious way any of the proofs in this release' and has not checked that the Lean compiles or that the challenge statement captures the problem; Kalai's post (7 Oct) summarises the claim with no check; erdosproblems.com/3 (last edited 4 Apr 2026, before the release) and its forum thread show no post about this claim as of my fetch.

machine_checked.note: The Comparator statement file's only theorem (manuscriptReciprocalProgressionTheorem) has `sorry` at line 32–33, so that file does not prove the claim. The proofs are in lean/OAI/Combinatorics/Progressions/Results/Conclusions.lean (manuscript_main_theorems and its two components) and Results/Reciprocal.lean, which contain no sorry in the files read, but their dependencies are in about 98 imported modules not inspected here. No compile result is reported in any source read. Bloom: 'I have not checked that the formalisation compiles'.

events.directly_checkable: The claim is an upper bound over all subsets of {1,…,N}, so there is no object to check by hand. The Lean statements are in the repository (Model.lean for definitions; Results/Conclusions.lean for the theorems).
events.doubts: (1) The formal layer and the headline disagree. The headline is exp(−(log N)^{c_k}); the Lean definition quoted from Model.lean is C·N·exp(−c·(log log N)^{1+η}). Bloom's post calls the Lean bound weaker, which is correct against the headline. But on my reading of the formula, exp(−c(log log N)^{1+η}) with η>0 decays faster than Leng–Sah–Sawhney's exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}) with c_k<1, so it would be stronger than the published k≥5 result, not weaker. Either the transcription, the sign or η's range is not what I read, or the formal layer proves something stronger than any published bound. This needs to be resolved by reading Model.lean in full before the Lean layer is credited with anything. (2) The formal repository's docs say the formalisation proves the reciprocal-sum consequence; the comparator file itself has sorry, which is consistent with a challenge statement but not with a completed proof at that path. (3) No named human has checked the 198-page argument in any source I read. (4) The paper's text was not readable, so its own statement of method, authorship and AI use is not in this record. (5) A secondary report (OfficeChai) says a group of external mathematicians including Bloom checked the proof and co-wrote a companion paper, and that Will Sawin made the exponent explicit. Bloom's own post says he has not looked at the proofs seriously and mentions no companion paper, and the only 2026 Sawin explicit-exponent work I found (arXiv:2605.20579) concerns the unit-distance problem. I could not confirm either claim. (6) The OpenAI README warns that 'some of the unformalized results could have issues'. This family has formal files, but the headline bound is not among the formalised statements.
events.direction: Claimed upper bound on r_k(N) for every k≥3, quasipolynomial in log N, which would move the upper bound for k≥4 far past Leng–Sah–Sawhney and reach the reciprocal-sum consequence. It cuts toward smaller r_k(N) and does not contradict any assertion in the bullet. It does not determine the growth rate, since no matching lower bound is claimed.

Family 159 is not named in the README's list of exceptions (a human-edited Riemann zeta writeup and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties). The family's own doc (lean/docs/159.md) names no model. The README also says 'Some outputs build upon earlier results produced by the models.' So the attribution of the Family 159 mathematics to the model rests on the repository-wide statement, not on a family-level sentence. The paper's own author/AI statement was unreadable.
systems.basis_quote: The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model.

events.what_happened: The manuscript 'Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions' (OpenAI, September 23, 2026) proves an upper bound on rₖ(N), the largest progression-free subset of {1,…,N}, for every fixed k ≥ 3: rₖ(N) ≤ Cₖ·N·exp(−cₖ(log N)^εₖ), with positive constants depending only on k. This is a stretched-exponential saving in log N. The title's 'quasipolynomial' refers to the equivalent density threshold log N ≥ Aₖ(2+log(1/α))^Aₖ for a set of density α to contain a k-term progression, which the manuscript states as an equivalent form of its main theorem. The manuscript proves no new lower bound on rₖ(N). Its only lower bound is Behrend's construction for k = 3, quoted as prior work: r₃(N) ≥ N·exp(−C√(log N)). A companion coloring corollary, Wᵣ(k) ≤ exp(Aₖ(2+log r)^Aₖ), follows from the same bound, and the lower bound that makes it two-sided is from the companion paper, not this one.
events.delivers: The upper half of the growth-rate question, for each fixed k ≥ 3: rₖ(N)/N ≤ Cₖ·exp(−cₖ(log N)^εₖ) → 0, which is a stronger decay than Szemerédi's o(N). For k ≥ 5 it improves the Leng–Sah–Sawhney saving exp(−(log log N)^cₖ), and for k = 4 it improves Green and Tao's N/(log N)^c. For k = 3 the text claims no improvement of the three-term exponent, so the existing bounds (Kelley–Meka, Bloom–Sisask, Raghavan) are not claimed to be beaten. The manuscript does not claim the growth rate of rₖ(N) is determined, and it does not claim the exact growth rate.
events.remains: (a) Upper bound: supplied for each k ≥ 3, but with the exponent εₖ unspecified. (b) Lower bound of the form N·gₖ(N) for k ≥ 3: not supplied by this manuscript; the only one stated is the cited Behrend bound for k = 3, and none is stated for k ≥ 4. (c) That the two bounds match, so that the growth rate is determined: not claimed. If the upper bound is correct, the question of the exact growth rate, and of the matching lower bound, remains open.

machine_checked.scope:
Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture asks whether every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The formalization proves this statement: for every requested length, such a set contains a progression with positive common difference.

The selected theorem is the reciprocal-sum consequence. The paper's quantitative upper bound for the largest progression-free subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is outside this statement.

events.doubts: (1) The constants Cₖ, cₖ, εₖ and Aₖ are asserted to exist, with no values given, and the text says the exponent is not optimized. (2) The title and abstract say 'quasipolynomial', but the bound itself is stated in log N form. Any reader comparing it with a growth-rate result should treat 'quasipolynomial' as referring to the density threshold. (3) The central width-recurrence argument is set out schematically, as described under the Erdős entry, and the same doubt applies here.; conditional on: The upper bound is conditional on the same external inputs as the matched Erdős entry: the quasipolynomial inverse theorem of Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17994, Theorem 1.2 and the appendix results cited from it), the radius-sensitive almost-periodicity theorem of Schoen and Sisask (arXiv:1408.2568, Theorem 5.4), and the other cited inputs listed there. The lower bound for k = 3 is Behrend's construction, which the manuscript cites and does not prove.
events.direction: improves the upper bound (stretched-exponential saving for every fixed k ≥ 3); no lower bound

origin.family_title: Erdős’s reciprocal-sum conjecture and quasipolynomial Szemerédi bounds

disputes.summary: Integer lower bound for r_3(N): Hunter's v1 (29 Jan 2024) claims 'the first quasipolynomial improvement since the original construction of Behrend'; Elsholtz–Hunter–Proske–Sauermann (18 Jun 2024) claim 'the first improvement upon Behrend's 1946 construction beyond lower-order factors'. Hunter's v3 says the results were merged with Elsholtz, Proske and Sauermann, and the June paper states that it replaces both earlier manuscripts. The record does not pick a winner; both events are recorded separately.

Secondary reports (OfficeChai, a 9 Oct 2026 article) credit this claim to a companion paper by external mathematicians including Thomas Bloom and say Will Sawin later made the exponent explicit. Bloom's 8 Oct 2026 post says he has not looked at the proofs seriously and names no companion paper; the Sawin explicit-exponent work found (arXiv:2605.20579) concerns the unit-distance problem. The attribution is unsupported in the sources I could read.

summary:
Searches (34 web queries, plus opened pages) and full-text reads turned up 14 events bearing on r_k(N), the window events of which are: Hunter's integer lower bound for k=3 (arXiv:2401.16106, v1 29 Jan 2024, three days after the freeze); Leng–Sah–Sawhney's upper bound N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}) for every k≥5 (arXiv:2402.17995, 28 Feb 2024, with companion 2402.17994); Elsholtz–Hunter–Proske–Sauermann's improved integer constant for k=3 (arXiv:2406.12290, 18 Jun 2024); Raghavan's k=3 upper-bound exponent 1/6 (arXiv:2603.27045, 27 Mar 2026); and the OpenAI repository's 198-page quasipolynomial claim for every k≥3 (family 159; repository commit 6 Oct 2026). Pre-window background events (Kelley–Meka 2023, Bloom–Sisask 2023, Leng 2023 for k=5, Green–Tao 2017 for k=4) are recorded as events too. Discounted as different questions: the finite-field lower bound (arXiv:2401.12802, 23 Jan 2024, pre-freeze), the corners theorem (arXiv:2504.07006), the primes (arXiv:2603.09281) and the finite-field ergodic constant (arXiv:2604.05768).

Close calls. (i) Hunter's v1 date sits three days after the freeze, so I placed it in the window; the earlier EPS preprint (23 Jan) is before it but concerns finite fields, so it is discounted on scope, not date. (ii) The OpenAI event: the folder name says 'September-23-2026', but the repository's only commit is 6 Oct 2026, so I dated the first public appearance to 6 Oct. (iii) Does the OpenAI claim move the quantity? It is a claimed upper bound on r_k(N) for all k≥3, so it moves the quantity on its face, but it is unchecked by any named expert, and its formal layer does not state the claimed bound. (iv) The AI attribution of Family 159: the README attributes 'the vast majority of results' to 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model' and does not name family 159 among its exceptions; the family's own doc names no model; I could not read the PDF's own authorship or AI statement. I put the README sentence in ai.systems because it is OpenAI's own account, but the family-level link is inferred from the repository-wide statement.

The Lean layer needs a flag for the later pass. The comparator file ErdosReciprocal.lean has `sorry` by design. The tactic proofs are in Results/Conclusions.lean and Results/Reciprocal.lean, which depend on about 98 imported modules I did not open. The quantitative definition in Model.lean is C·N·exp(−c(log log N)^{1+η}). Bloom calls this weaker than the headline, which it is. But on my reading, with η>0 it decays faster than LSS's exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}), so it would be stronger than the published k≥5 bound. That makes me suspect a transcription or sign issue. I have not resolved it.

AI involvement outside the mathematics: Harmonic's Aristotle is reported (OfficeChai, citing the release) as formalising proofs in Lean for the batch. That is formalisation, and I have not confirmed it for family 159 in a primary source, so it is not in ai.systems. Two claims of companion-paper checking and of a Sawin exponent are unsupported (see disputes). A 2026 human audit (arXiv:2608.14673, Sienicki and Sienicki) covers OpenAI's ten Astra results of 1 Aug 2026 and does not mention this problem; I opened it and recorded nothing from it for this bullet.

The growth rate itself is not determined by any event. Upper bounds for k=3 have moved (Kelley–Meka, Bloom–Sisask, Raghavan), for k≥4 they have moved (Green–Tao for k=4, Leng–Sah–Sawhney for k≥5, and the 2026 claim), and lower bounds moved only for k=3 (Hunter; EHPS). The lower-bound gap remains for every k; Rankin's 1961 construction is still the k≥4 lower bound as cited by Wikipedia. My search found no AI-driven change to any of these bounds: the AlphaEvolve and FunSearch results found are about the sum–difference problem, Ramsey numbers and the finite-field cap set, which are not r_k(N) on {1,…,N}.
competing_reading: Reading the OpenAI event as moving the problem: it is a claim of r_k(N) ≤ N·exp(−(log N)^{c_k}) for every k≥3, a change of the upper bound's form for every k≥4, and it contains the reciprocal-sum consequence. Against that, the claim is unchecked, the Lean definition in the repository states a different and possibly stronger-looking bound, and no lower bound changes, so the growth rate is not determined. The LSS k≥5 result by itself would be read as moving the problem only for k≥5, leaving k=3 and k=4 open. A judge who requires a result for all k at once would count none of the upper-bound events as determining the growth rate; a judge who counts improvements of the bound would count several.
what_would_settle_it: For the OpenAI event: a named expert's written check of the 198-page PDF's main quantitative theorem, or a sorry-free Lean proof of the exp(−(log N)^{c_k}) statement with its dependencies compiled, together with a corrected reading of Model.lean (the sign and range of η) and the PDF's own authorship and AI-use statement. For the growth question: a matching lower bound at the quasipolynomial scale for some k≥4, or a determined constant in either direction for any k. For the k=3 scope in Raghavan's paper: the setting of the headline theorem ({1,…,N} or ℤ/Nℤ).

event.what_happened: Zach Hunter, 'New lower bounds for r_3(N)' (arXiv:2401.16106), v1 submitted Monday 29 Jan 2024. Develops ideas of Elsholtz, Proske and Sauermann to construct denser subsets of {1,…,N} with no 3-term progression. Abstract: 'This gives the first quasipolynomial improvement since the original construction of Behrend.' v3 (2 Jul 2024) states that the results have been merged with Elsholtz, Proske and Sauermann (arXiv:2401.12802).
event.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2024; v2 30 Jan 2024; v3 2 Jul 2024 (adds the merger note; the merged paper is arXiv:2406.12290).
event.delivers: Only k=3, on the integers: a lower bound r_3(N) ≫ N·2^{−(c+o(1))·2√(2 log₂ N)} with c = √(log₂√(32/9)) ≈ 0.9567 (as stated in the v3 Theorem 1). Behrend's construction has c=1 in the same form, so this improves the constant in the Behrend-type lower bound. It is not a change to the order of exp(−c√log N). The v1 abstract, read directly, claims the improvement on {1,…,N}.
event.remains: The exact growth rate of r_3(N), i.e. the gap between this lower bound and the k=3 upper bounds. All k≥4 lower bounds, which are unchanged (Rankin 1961 and O'Bryant as cited by Wikipedia).
event.time_since_posted: About 32 months to 11 Oct 2026. The merged successor (June 2024) is the paper cited in later work; no journal reference found for either.
event.direction: Lower bound for 3-AP-free subsets of {1,…,N}, improving the Behrend constant. Cuts toward larger r_3(N). No counterexample to anything the bullet asserts.
event.object: An explicit construction of subsets of {1,…,N} free of 3-term progressions, of size N·2^{−(c+o(1))·2√(2 log₂N)} with c ≈ 0.9567 (Theorem 1 of v3). It is built by adapting the Elsholtz–Proske–Sauermann construction in place of Behrend's sphere-based set. The abstract's word 'construct' is the basis for calling it explicit; I did not check the proof line by line.

judgement.why: The statement asks to determine the growth rate of r_k(N); no event supplies matching upper and lower bounds for any k, so every substantive event is a bound (F4), including the post-snapshot ones: Hunter and EHPS (k=3 Behrend constant), LSS (k>=5 upper bound), Raghavan (k=3 exponent 1/6) and the OpenAI claim (stretched-exponential upper bound for all k>=3). I did not score per-k bounds as 'case', since even for a single k nothing is determined. Hunter's v1 of 29 Jan 2024 is three days after the snapshot. EPS (finite groups), corners, primes and the finite-field ergodic constant are variants; the LSS inverse theorem is a tool with no bound of its own (none). Kalai's digest of EHPS describes the result without a check, so EHPS stays unreviewed. The two OpenAI rows describe one release, judged identically: AI-generated per the README's repository-wide statement (family 159 is not among the named exceptions), doubtful but not set aside.
judgement.doubts: The two OpenAI events duplicate one release. Its AI attribution rests on a repository-wide README sentence, not a family-level statement. The second OpenAI entry says k=3's exponent is not improved, so for k=3 it is no bound advance; the claim moves k>=4. Raghavan's setting ({1..N} vs Z/NZ) is unresolved but immaterial to the scope.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
